name: hair

attributes.attribute: ritual and spiritual symbol of the ancient Celts
long and lime-treated for warriors, long and braided for women
never thrown into fire for fear of fever
sign of fairy blood in the veins
animal hair bound on a dog bite to ensure healing

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Hair was an important ritual and spiritual symbol to the ancient Celts. Warriors wore their hair long and their mustaches untrimmed in battle. Some treated the hair with lime to make a fearfully wild appearance. Women kept their hair long, often braided, as a mark of their sexual power. Druids wore a special tonsure that set them apart from the tribe. Folklore kept the power of hair alive. People never threw cut or combed hair into a fire, fearing they would get a fever. This is magical part-equals-whole thinking. Red hair mattered most, for it showed fairy blood ran in the veins. Mermaids lured sailors by combing their hair. By sympathetic magic it was dangerous for a girl to comb her hair while her brothers were at sea. Animal hair also carried power, especially horse hair, which could come alive in water. A dog bite had to be bound with hair from the animal to ensure healing.
objective: Document hair as a ritual and spiritual symbol of the ancient Celts.
key_results: Record its ritual use by warriors, women, and Druids.
List the hair superstitions of fire, red hair, and sympathetic magic.
Note the power of animal hair in healing and mermaid lure.
evidence: Monaghan, P. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore (2008): hair entry.
